catalog_quote: Stress is non-contrastive on the phonological word level. The majority of the phonological words are pronounced with stress on the first and alternately following syllables. However, there are exceptions. ... Some phonemes and combinations of phonemes are stronger than others. If the second syllable consists of a combination of phonemes greater* in strength than the first syllable, the second syllable takes the stress rather than the first in two and three syllable words, except in three syllable words when the last syllable has a complex nuclei, and the first two have simple nuclei with the first syllable the weakest. Then, the stress returns to first and third, with the strongest stress on the third syllable. In 4-syllable words when the second syllable has the strongest combination, the stress also returns to first and third syllables. ... Because the greatest tendency is to stress first and third syllables, when the strength of the first and second syllable or even if the first may be slightly weaker, the stress often comes on the first syllable, is even, or there is fluctuation. ... (hu'ra) /hura/ fly -- The hu combination being very weak and the ra a strong combination, the stress is always on the second syllable.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not contrastive. By default the phonological word is stressed on its first syllable, with alternating (secondary) stresses on the following odd syllables (1st, 3rd..). The default is overridden by a phoneme-'strength' hierarchy: if the second syllable is markedly stronger than the first (strong consonant d/b/g/r/t/p/k plus strong vowel e/a/o/u, a complex nucleus VV, or a CVC/CCVC syllable, versus a weak first syllable such as hu, wu, nɨ, hɨ), the second syllable takes the stress in 2- and 3-syllable words (hu'ra 'fly', nɨ'duwi 'sit down'); when a strong third syllable with a complex nucleus follows two simple ones, stress returns to 1st+3rd with the strongest on the 3rd ('nɨdu'kai); 4-syllable words revert to 1st+3rd ('yɨkrɨp'kiyɨn). Where the strength difference is small, stress often stays initial, is even, or fluctuates. The authors' own summary is initial-with-alternation; the exceptions are a weight/sonority attraction, so 'weight-sensitive' is a defensible alternative reading. The 2004 SIL OPD sheet condenses this to 'Stress is usually on the first syllable.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Alternating: 'stress on the first and alternately following syllables' (1st, 3rd..); in some 3-syllable words the strongest stress falls on the 3rd syllable ('nɨdu'kai 'sit down (inside)'). Each component of a compound keeps its own stress (a grammatical compound 'remains two (or more) phonological words'); the second part gets higher pitch.
new_statements.exceptions: Second-syllable stress when the 2nd syllable is phonemically 'stronger' than the 1st (2- and 3-syllable words; e.g. /hura/ 'fly', /nɨduwi/ 'sit down', /nɨkrɨpki/ 'cut (pres.)'); 1st+3rd pattern restored in 4-syllable words and when a strong complex-nucleus 3rd syllable follows two simple syllables; fluctuation or even stress when strengths are close (/nɨdidi/ 'afraid', /hɨdi/ 'four'); compounds keep component stresses. Tone non-contrastive: stressed syllables generally high, unstressed low (p. 53).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (authors' term), citation/wordlist forms from ~1000 words gathered in conversation at Yawenian village, 1969-1970; intonation (sec. 5.4) treated separately: pause-group nucleus has highest pitch and stress, usually on the verb.
new_statements.identity_note: Statement describes Sepik Iwam [iws] = sepi1255 as spoken at Yawenian village (data 1969-1970, ~1000 words; villages Yawenian, Oum I, Oum II, Tauri, Iniok). May River Iwam [iwm] = iwam1256 is a separate language (the SIL OPD for it says 'stress is phonemic at the word level', and Conrad 1972's contrastive-stress footnote is about May River Iwam despite SIL/Glottolog filing that article under iws) - do not merge the two statements.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not contrastive. The default is stress on the first syllable and on every alternate syllable after it (1st, 3rd..). A second syllable that is phonologically 'stronger' than the first (strong consonant t/p/k/d/b/g/r + full vowel, or a VV/CVV/CVC/CCVC syllable, versus a weak first syllable such as hu, wu, hwu, nɨ, hɨ or a bare V) takes the stress instead of the first in two- and three-syllable words (hu'ra 'fly', nɨ'duwi 'sit down'); in three-syllable words whose final syllable has a complex nucleus the stress goes back to 1st + 3rd with the strongest on the 3rd ('nɨdu'kai), and in four-syllable words it goes back to 1st + 3rd ('yɨkrɨp'kiyɨn). Where the strength difference is small the stress is often initial, even, or fluctuates ('hɨdi ~ 'hɨ'di ~ hɨ'di 'four'). Tone is non-contrastive; stressed syllables are generally high-pitched.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Alternating: stress on the first and 'alternately following' syllables; in 3-syllable words with a heavy final syllable the stresses fall on 1st and 3rd with the strongest on the 3rd; compound words keep the stresses of each component and remain two or more phonological words, the second part getting higher intonation (p. 53).
new_statements.exceptions: Stronger second syllable takes the stress in 2-3 syllable words; heavy final syllable of 3-syllable words and all 4-syllable words revert to 1st + 3rd; 'Fluctuation also occurs in three syllable words when the second syllable is not sufficiently stronger than the first to always override it' (p. 52); the authors flag that further study is needed to quantify how much stronger the second syllable must be (footnote p. 51).
new_statements.identity_note: Laszlo & Rehburg 1970 describe Sepik Iwam as spoken in the village of Yawenian (villages listed: Yawenian, Oum I, Oum II, Tauri, Iniok; ~1600 speakers; data 1969-1970, ~1000 words), explicitly set apart from May River Iwam (Conrad's dialect). Conrad & Dye 1975: 12 fn. 21 identify Laycock 1965's 'Iwam' phonology as Sepik Iwam, while Glottolog/WALS tag the Laycock reference with iwm (May River Iwam); LAPSyD files its Laycock 1965 stress remark under May River Iwam.
